description:
Explore Lady Macbeth’s most important quotes from Macbeth in this Animated Classics Shakespeare video, perfect for understanding her role, ambition, power and tragic downfall.

Lady Macbeth begins the play as one of Shakespeare’s most forceful and persuasive characters. When she hears Macbeth may become king, she immediately pushes him towards murder, challenging his courage and masculinity so that he will kill Duncan. At first, she appears controlled, ruthless and determined, but Shakespeare gradually reveals the emotional cost of guilt. As Macbeth becomes more violent and distant, Lady Macbeth loses the power she once had over him. Her famous sleepwalking scene shows her mind overwhelmed by guilt, as she imagines blood on her hands that cannot be washed away.

Exam-ready character analysis

Lady Macbeth represents ambition, manipulation, gender expectations, guilt and psychological collapse. Early in the play, she rejects traditional ideas of femininity and asks to be filled with cruelty so she can carry out violent thoughts. She is central to Duncan’s murder, but unlike Macbeth, she cannot continue living with the consequences. Her journey moves from control to vulnerability, from confidence to fear, and finally from denial to mental illness caused by guilt.

Key quote meanings

“Come, you spirits that tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here”
Lady Macbeth asks supernatural forces to remove her feminine softness and fill her with cruelty. This shows her rejection of expected female behaviour and her desire for power.

“Look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under’t”
She tells Macbeth to appear innocent while hiding evil intentions. This is one of the clearest quotes about deception and appearance versus reality.

“When you durst do it, then you were a man”
Lady Macbeth attacks Macbeth’s masculinity to manipulate him into murdering Duncan. She uses shame as a weapon.

“A little water clears us of this deed”
At first, Lady Macbeth believes guilt can be washed away easily. This becomes deeply ironic later when she cannot stop imagining blood on her hands.

“Nought’s had, all’s spent, where our desire is got without content”
Lady Macbeth realises that getting what they wanted has not brought happiness or peace. Power has come at a terrible emotional cost.

“Out, damned spot! Out, I say!”
In the sleepwalking scene, Lady Macbeth imagines blood on her hands. Her guilt has become impossible to escape, showing her mental collapse.

“What, will these hands ne’er be clean?”
This directly reverses her earlier confidence that “a little water” could clear them. She now understands that guilt cannot be physically washed away.

“All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”
Lady Macbeth feels permanently stained by guilt. The image suggests that no luxury, beauty or power can cover the moral corruption of murder.

Lady Macbeth’s tragedy is that she believes she can control evil, but once Duncan is murdered, guilt begins to destroy her from within.

Revise the most important GCSE quotes from Macbeth with this complete animated guide, perfect for GCSE and A Level English Literature, starring Brian Cox and Zoe Wanermaker.

⏱️ Macbeth Key Quotes & Analysis

00:00 – “When shall we three meet again?” / “Fair is foul, and foul is fair”
Introduces the supernatural and theme of moral confusion, where appearances are deceptive. This sets the tone for the entire play and Macbeth’s eventual downfall.

00.55 – “What he hath lost, noble Macbeth hath won”
Establishes Macbeth as a heroic figure at the start, making his later corruption more tragic and highlighting Shakespeare’s warning about power.

01.22 – “All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter!”
The witches plant the idea of ambition, showing how external influences can trigger internal desire and drive the plot forward.

02.28 – “Stars, hide your fires; let not light see my black and deep desires”
Reveals Macbeth’s inner conflict and growing ambition, linking to themes of darkness, secrecy and evil intentions.

02.52 – “Is this a dagger which I see before me?”
A key moment of psychological conflict, showing Macbeth’s descent into madness and the influence of the supernatural or his guilty imagination.

03.28 – “A little water clears us of this deed”
Lady Macbeth downplays guilt, contrasting later with her breakdown and reinforcing the theme that guilt cannot be escaped.

04.02 – “O, full of scorpions is my mind”
Highlights Macbeth’s tormented mental state, suggesting that power has brought fear rather than security.

04.40 – Banquo’s ghost scene
Represents guilt and paranoia, showing how Macbeth is psychologically haunted by his actions and losing control.

05.43 – “Out, damned spot!”
Lady Macbeth’s guilt manifests physically, symbolising that crime cannot be hidden and guilt consumes the mind.

06.40 – “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow…”
A powerful reflection on life’s meaninglessness, showing Macbeth’s despair and the ultimate consequences of his actions.

Experience The Tempest by William Shakespeare in this engaging animated retelling of one of his most celebrated plays.

After being betrayed and cast adrift, Prospero lives on a mysterious island with his daughter Miranda. When his enemies sail nearby, he summons a powerful storm, setting in motion a story of magic, betrayal, love and forgiveness.

This animated adaptation brings the drama and themes of The Tempest to life through clear storytelling and striking visuals, offering a fresh way to experience Shakespeare’s final play.

🌊 Featuring:
• Prospero and his magic
• The shipwreck and storm
• Ariel and Caliban
• Miranda and Ferdinand
• Themes of power and redemption

A timeless Shakespeare classic presented through animation.
About Animated Classics

Animated Classics brings timeless stories to life through exciting and diverse animation techniques. From Shakespeare’s plays and great operas to Bible stories, global folk tales and the teachings of world faiths, the channel is a rich and visually captivating resource for viewers of all ages.

Revise two of the most studied Shakespeare plays for GCSE English Literature in this Animated Classics double feature, featuring Romeo and Juliet and Macbeth back to back.

These award winning animated adaptations bring Shakespeare’s stories to life in a clear and engaging way, helping you understand plot, characters and key themes while preparing for exam season.

Romeo and Juliet explores love, conflict and fate as two young lovers are torn apart by the rivalry between their families.

Macbeth follows the rise and fall of a noble soldier whose ambition leads him down a dark path of guilt, power and destruction.

📚 Ideal for GCSE revision across AQA, Edexcel, OCR and WJEC, this compilation is perfect for rewatching key scenes, refreshing your knowledge of the story and revising themes before exams.

Animated Classics brings timeless stories to life through exciting and diverse animation techniques. From Shakespeare’s plays and great operas to Bible stories, global folk tales and the teachings of world faiths, this channel is a rich and visually captivating resource for viewers of all ages.
